question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

claims.text: For the adjacency matrix A of a simple undirected graph on N vertices: the sum of row i (and of column i) is the degree of n_i, the number of edges at n_i; and the sum of all entries is 2|E|. Proof: A_ij = 1 exactly when n_j is a neighbour of n_i; in a simple graph each neighbour is joined to n_i by exactly one edge and there are no loops, so the number of 1s in row i is the number of edges at n_i; summing over i counts every edge twice (once from each end). Checked on the board matrix: row sums 1, 2, 1, total 4 = 2|E| with |E| = 2.

support.quote: Degree of vi is equal to the sum of the off diagonal entries plus twice the diagonal entries.

claims.text: In a simple graph a walk is determined by its vertex sequence u_0, u_1, ..., u_k, because between two vertices there is at most one edge and the textbook's walk requires e_i = u_{i-1}u_i. Hence the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j equals the number of vertex sequences w_0 = n_i, w_1, ..., w_k = n_j with every consecutive pair adjacent. The induction proof of the walk-counting theorem counts these sequences.

A walk (in G) means a finite sequence (v0 , v1 , . . . , vk ) of vertices of G (with k ≥ 0) such that all of v0 v1 , v1 v2 , v2 v3 , . . . , vk−1 vk are edges of G.

claims.text: Full induction proof of the walk-counting theorem (Theorem 1): for every positive integer k and all i, j, (A^k)_ij is the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j. Base case k = 1: a walk of length 1 from n_i to n_j is the pair (n_i, n_j), which exists (once) iff the two are adjacent, i.e. the count is A_ij = (A^1)_ij. Inductive step: split the walks of length k from n_i to n_j by their second-last vertex n_r; deleting the last vertex is a bijection between those walks and the walks of length k-1 from n_i to n_r, available exactly when A_rj = 1; so the count with second-last vertex n_r is (A^(k-1))_ir A_rj by the hypothesis; summing over r gives sum_r (A^(k-1))_ir A_rj = (A^k)_ij. The proof is the standard route recorded in C7 and is written out in full in the module report. Not relied on: any statement in paramadevan2021adjacency Theorem 1 (see C11).

support.quote: Let A be the adjacency matrix of a simple graph G on vertices v1 , v2 , . . . , vn . Let k be a positive integer. Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.
Thus the total number of walks of length k from vi to vj is the sum of the expressions (Ak−1 )ir Arj over all vertices vr of G, which is exactly (Ak )ij .

claims.text: Walk-versus-path counterexample on the board graph, computed: (A^2)_11 = 1, and the one closed walk of length 2 at n_1 is 1-2-1, which repeats the vertex n_1 and the edge n_1n_2, so it is neither a path (Definition 1.2.13, distinct vertices) nor a trail (Definition 1.2.12, distinct edges). Second counterexample: (A^3)_12 = 2, the walks being 1-2-1-2 and 1-2-3-2, yet there is no path or trail of length 3 from n_1 to n_2; the only path from n_1 to n_2 has length 1. By script, among walks 1 to 2 the number of paths is 1, 0, 0, 0, 0 for k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 while the walk counts are 1, 0, 2, 0, 4 (k = 5: 4 walks).

claims.text: Corollaries of the walk-counting theorem: (a) every entry of A^k is a non-negative integer, so a sum of such matrices has a positive entry iff some summand does; (b) (A^k)_ij > 0 iff a walk of length exactly k from n_i to n_j exists; (c) A^k is symmetric for every k >= 1, because (A^k)^T = (A^T)^k = A^k, equivalently because reversing a walk is a bijection between walks from n_i to n_j and walks from n_j to n_i (this uses that the graph is undirected). Part (c) was also checked by script on the board matrix for k = 1..6.

support.quote: Let A be the adjacency matrix of a simple graph G on vertices v1 , v2 , . . . , vn . Let k be a positive integer. Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.

claims.text: Where the hypotheses are used in the proof: simplicity (no loops, no repeated edges) makes each A_rj equal to the number of edges between n_r and n_j, hence 0 or 1, and makes a walk equal to its vertex sequence; undirectedness is not used by the induction itself (only symmetry of A, which gives corollary (c)). For a multigraph the same proof counts walks with multiplicity if A_rj is the number of edges. This agrees with the sources that state the theorem for digraphs and multidigraphs (C6).
